title: kv-cache reuse/eviction/paging memory-bandwidth investigation
body:
Summary:

This doc captures the investigation into KV cache behavior observed in several recent throughput/latency regressions with long-context chat workloads. Primary focus: measured reuse rates, eviction behavior, paging events, and host memory / PCIe memory-bandwidth impacts. This is a working note (profiling artifacts attached via linked_artifacts).

Motivation / Background:
- Multiple customer and internal benchmarks show increased p50/p95 token latency when sequence lengths > 8k tokens and throughput is moderate-to-high.
- Hypothesis: KV cache eviction and subsequent re-population (paging) is causing repeated KV loads from GPU/CPU memory leading to bandwidth saturation and tail latency spikes.
- Goal: quantify reuse, eviction rate, paging frequency, and memory bandwidth at different workload shapes and cache configs; recommend mitigations.

Hypotheses:
1) Low reuse for certain multi-turn chat patterns (many short unique prefixes) causes frequent cache churn and unnecessary re-embedding of KV state.
2) Eviction policy (LRU-ish) plus fixed per-shard memory budgets leads to worst-case pathological thrashing under some request mixes.
3) Paging (spill to host) increases host<->GPU memory bandwidth and PCIe latency, causing token emission tail spikes.

Experimental setup:
- Code: serving-runtime branch kv-cache-profiling-2026-05 (see PR linked)
- Hardware: p4d.24xlarge-like instance (NVIDIA A100 equivalent), PCIe Gen4 NVLink disabled for reproducibility.
- Model: LLaMA-2-13B (quantized fp16 runtime path) with KV cache enabled.
- Configs tested: cache_size_per_shard = [6GB, 8GB, 12GB], eviction_policy = [LRU, segmented-LRU], reserve_prefetch = [true,false], allow_paging = [true,false]
- Workloads: 1) long-single-turn (1x 16k token prompt), 2) multi-turn-greedy (chain of 10 turns, each ~1.6k tokens with unique prefixes), 3) short-turn-high-QPS (many short 64-token queries from multiple users).
- Metrics captured: reuse_rate (fraction of KV reads that hit cached KV entries), eviction_rate (evictions/sec), paging_events (host->gpu transfers/sec), gpu_mem_bw (GB/s), host_mem_bw (GB/s), token_latency_p50/p95/p99 (ms), tokens/sec throughput.

Definitions / measurement notes:
- reuse_rate computed from KV lookup counters: hits / (hits + misses) over a sliding window.
- eviction_rate measured from eviction callback count per second.
- paging_events measured via our tracer: count of spill/load operations between GPU and host.
- memory bandwidth measured via nvprof-like counters aggregated during run windows.

Key results (representative):
- Workload: multi-turn-greedy, cache_size=8GB, eviction=LRU, allow_paging=true:
  - reuse_rate: 32%
  - eviction_rate: 420 evictions/sec per shard
  - paging_events: 380 loads/sec, 390 spills/sec
  - gpu_mem_bw: 120 GB/s sustained (peaks 210 GB/s on spikes)
  - host_mem_bw: 48 GB/s
  - token_latency_p95: +85% over baseline (no-paging run)
  - throughput: -28% vs no-paging run

- Workload: multi-turn-greedy, cache_size=12GB, eviction=segmented-LRU, allow_paging=true:
  - reuse_rate: 61%
  - eviction_rate: 120 evictions/sec per shard
  - paging_events: 95 loads/sec, 110 spills/sec
  - gpu_mem_bw: 70 GB/s
  - host_mem_bw: 22 GB/s
  - token_latency_p95: +12% over baseline
  - throughput: -6% vs baseline

- Workload: short-turn-high-QPS, cache_size=8GB, allow_paging=false:
  - reuse_rate: 8%
  - eviction_rate: 980 evictions/sec per shard
  - paging_events: 0
  - gpu_mem_bw: 180 GB/s (higher due to repeated KV rebuild ops)
  - token_latency_p95: +90% (tail latency dominated by cache rebuild work on GPU)

Observations / Interpretation:
- Reuse rate correlates strongly with working set size vs cache size and with request prefix locality. Low reuse -> high eviction and rebuild work.
- When allow_paging=true, paging reduces immediate OOM risk but moves pressure to host<->GPU bandwidth; paging introduces latency variance due to PCIe transfers (esp. for large KV pages).
- Segmented-LRU with a slightly larger cache reduces eviction and paging substantially, improving p95 and throughput.
- For short-turn-high-QPS workloads, even disabling paging does not help because the working set is simply too large and transient; the runtime does a lot of recompute to rebuild KV and saturates GPU memory bandwidth.
- NVLink / intra-node connectivity and PCIe version materially change absolute numbers; our test env (no NVLink) is a conservative worst-case.

Root cause(s):
- The eviction cadence + large KV page size means we evict coarse-grained chunks that are likely to be partially reused shortly after eviction, causing repeated full-page reloads.
- Paging unit size and lack of async prefetch in current path causes stalls while waiting for PCIe transfers.
- Eviction algorithm does not account for per-conversation temporal locality patterns (e.g., keep recent-turn small entries pinned).

Potential mitigations evaluated and preliminary results:
1) Reduce paging unit size (split large pages into smaller subpages): decreases peak pci transfer size; in tests reduced p95 by ~20% but increased CPU overhead for bookkeeping.
2) Segmented-LRU / adaptive hot-list: keep a small hot list (1-2% of cache) pinned for recent turns -> reuse_rate up ~+18-25pp.
3) Opportunistic prefetch: upon detecting conversational pattern, prefetch next likely KV segments asynchronously -> reduced stalls in 70% of simulated cases.
4) Dynamic cache resizing by workload class (auto-increase reserved cache for multi-turn chat): helps but needs admission control to avoid cross-tenant interference.
5) Eviction smoothing (stagger evictions across microbatches) to avoid bursty bandwidth spikes.

Tradeoffs and costs:
- Smaller page sizes reduce PCIe latency but increase metadata footprint and CPU cycles for managing more objects.
- Prefetch requires accurate prediction heuristics to avoid wasted bandwidth.
- Segmented-LRU/hot-list raises memory fragmentation and may complicate memory accounting for Dedicated/Private customers with strict bounds.

Recommended short-term actions (next 2 weeks):
- Implement segmented-LRU with 2% hot-list and run A/B on production-like load (owner: Priya); target: reduce eviction_rate by 50% for multi-turn workloads.
- Add async prefetch path prototype gated by config flag; test with deterministic chat patterns (owner: Ethan).
- Reduce default page size used for kernel uploads by 2x in staging; measure CPU overhead and p95 improvements (owner: Zoe).

Recommended mid-term actions (1-3 months):
- Add workload-aware cache sizing policy (auto-reserve for conversation-heavy routes) with admission control and observability (metrics + traces).
- Enhance eviction heuristics to consider conversation id and recent access frequency (approx LFU hybrid).
- If feasible, exploit NVLink / GPU-peer paths in Dedicated deployments for high-throughput customers and document performance delta.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- What is the incidence of these pathological request mixes in production? Add sampled telemetry to measure real reuse rates per-route.
- How much does model architecture (decoder-only vs. other variants) change page size sensitivity?
- Cost impact: estimate increased CPU and memory metadata cost vs. expected token-cost savings for customers.

Appendix A: raw sample traces (short):
- trace-2026-05-11-1332: shows back-to-back evictions preventing reuse for conversation X; attached in linked_artifacts.
- nvprof-window-1: GPU BW heatmap for multi-turn-greedy run.

Appendix B: checklist to run replications:
1) checkout branch kv-cache-profiling-2026-05
2) run bench script bench/kv_cache_profile.sh --workload multi-turn-greedy --cache 8GB --eviction LRU
3) collect traces: /tmp/kv-profiling/<run-id>
4) upload perf artifacts to S3 and attach to Jira JIRA-SRV-8765

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working investigation; numbers are representative but not finalized. Please sanity-check the suggested mitigations and flag any customer impact concerns.

Action owners recap:
- Priya Shah: segmented-LRU prototype and production A/B plan
- Ethan Martinez: async prefetch prototype and microbench harness
- Zoe Kim: page-size change testing and CPU overhead analysis

-- end --
